Alleviation of ammonia inhibition via nano-bubble water supplementation 
during anaerobic digestion of ammonia-rich swine manure: Buffering 
capacity promotion and methane production enhancement 
Yujie Fan a, Xiaojing Yang a, Zhongfang Lei b, Zhenya Zhang b, Motoyoshi Kobayashi b, 
Yasuhisa Adachi b, Kazuya Shimizu b,* 
a Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan 
b Faculty of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan   
H I G H L I G H T S  
• Ammonia inhibition was alleviated under nano-bubble water (NBW) supplementation. 
• Extracellular hydrolases and coenzyme F420 were enhanced with NBW supplementation. 
• NBW supplementation promoted buffering capacity under ammonia inhibition. 
• CH4 production was enhanced by 12.3–38.7% by NBW supplementation. 
• NBW addition shortened the lag phase and increased the maximum CH4 production rate.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Swine manure 
Nano-bubble water 
Ammonia inhibition 
Buffering capacity 
A B S T R A C T   
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of ammonia-rich swine manure (SM) with nano-bubble water (NBW) supplementation 
was studied in this work with the expectation of ammonia inhibition alleviation, buffering capacity promotion, 
and methane production enhancement. Results indicated that cumulative methane yield was elevated by 
12.3–38.7% in NBW groups. Besides, the reduced methane production rate and elongated lag phase under 
ammonia inhibition were increased and shortened by NBW supplementation, respectively. The rapid increase of 
total alkalinity (TA) and partial alkalinity (PA) could be observed with NBW supplementation, as well as the 
rapid decline of VFA/TA, thus improved buffering capacity and alleviated ammonia inhibition. Moreover, higher 
level of extracellular hydrolases and coenzyme F420 could be detected in NBW groups. In conclusion, NBW with 
higher mobility and zeta potential (absolute value) could be a promising strategy for the alleviation of ammonia 
suppression during the AD of SM.   
1. Introduction 
Over 80 million tons of livestock manure are produced in Japan 
annually, among which the output of swine manure (SM) exceeds one- 
quarter of the total (around 21 million tons) (MAFF, 2019). To reduce 
the pollution in surrounding environment and increase the efficiency of 
biomass resources utilization, these enormous amounts of SM should be 
treated scientifically and effectively. Composting is widely applied to 
treat livestock manure due to its many advantages, such as increasing 
fertility and stabilizing organics (Yuan et al., 2017). However, 
composting has shortcomings like excessive carbon dioxide emissions 
and nutrient loss, which restrict its wider application in practice 
(Fukumoto et al., 2003). Compare to composting, anaerobic digestion 
(AD) shows various superiorities in solid reduction and energy produc­
tion when treating livestock manure (Li et al., 2020). However, 
ammonia inhibition occurs easily during AD processes due to the high 
nitrogen content of SM, which is not good for the progress of AD (Huang 
et al., 2019). If ammonia inhibition cannot be effectively alleviated, it 
will affect the AD system and reduce methane yield (Tian et al., 2019). 
Up to now, various methods have been applied in previous studies to

alleviate ammonia inhibition such as ammonia stripping (Yin et al., 
2019), membrane (Shi et al., 2020), microbial acclimation (Yan et al., 
2019) and struvite precipitation (Lorick et al., 2020). However, these 
technologies still have disadvantages, such as complexity of operation, 
energy consumption and secondary pollution. New strategies with easier 
operation processes and less chemical addition are desired for efficient 
alleviation of ammonia inhibition. As known, water plays a prominent 
role in the buffering and material transport for all the substrate and 
reactants (Kothari et al., 2014; Bollon et al., 2013). In this field, most of 
the previous reports focused on the impact of water content on the AD 
process, namely, the impact of different total solids (TS) on AD process 
(Indren et al., 2020; Latifi et al., 2019). However, few studies focused on 
the influence of water characteristics and types on the AD process under 
ammonia inhibition. It’s still unclear whether changing the types and 
characteristics of water would bring about improvement in AD perfor­
mance under ammonia inhibition. 
Nano-bubble water (NBW) has some unique characteristics such as 
high air solubility, improved mass transferability and generation of free 
radicals (Liu et al., 2019, 2013; Temesgen et al., 2017). NBW has been 
widely used in medicine (Hayashi et al., 2019), functional food (Guo 
et al., 2020), agriculture (Zhou et al., 2019), industry (Kim et al., 2020), 
and environmental engineering (Yu et al., 2019). Most recently, NBW 
was found to be able to promote methane production during the AD 
process as reported by many studies (Fan et al., 2020a; Yang et al., 
2020a). However, the above-mentioned promoting effect by NBW was 
achieved when no inhibition occurred. Considering the unique proper­
ties of NBW, it would be of great promise in alleviating ammonia inhi­
bition and enhancing methane production in the AD of ammonia-rich 
SM, without secondary pollution and exceeding energy consumption. 
Therefore, the purpose of this work was to elucidate the effect of 
NBW supplementation on the AD of ammonia-rich SM occurred varying 
degrees of ammonia inhibition, aiming at applying a new approach to 
alleviate ammonia inhibition and enhance methane production without 
using conventional methods. This research was the first attempt of 
applying NBW in the AD process of ammonia-rich SM. Results from this 
work are targeting a novel method to alleviate the inhibitory effect from 
ammonia, which often occurs during the AD process in ammonia-rich 
SM. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. AD tests 
2.1.1. SM and inoculum 
The fresh SM was directly collected from the medium-sized swine 
company in Tsukuba, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. Before stored at 4 ◦C for 
subsequent tests, this fresh SM was mixed thoroughly to obtain the 
representative SM sample. Digested sludge used for acclimatization of 
inoculum was directly taken from a sewage treatment plant in Ibaraki 
Prefecture, Japan in this work. The storage of directly collected digested 
sludge and the process of acclimatization of inoculum were conducted 
based on the previous report (Fan et al., 2020b). The main character­
istics of the fresh SM and inoculum were shown in Table 1. 
2.1.2. AD trials 
In this work, different amounts of NH4Cl were added to the reactors 
before the AD experiment to simulate different levels of ammonia in­
hibition. Eight groups of reactors were designed: NH4Cl (g) in R(0)Con­
trol/R(0)NBW; R(1)Control /R(1)NBW; R(3)Control /R(3)NBW; R(5)Control /R 
(5)NBW were addition to 0, 1 g, 3 g and 5 g, respectively. Each Scott 
Duran bottle (working volume 200 mL) was loaded with SM and inoc­
ulum, and the feed/microorganisms (VS basis) ratio was kept about 1:1. 
At the beginning of the tests, 100 mL NBW or deionized water (DW) 
were added into RNBW and RControl, respectively. To avoid the intro­
duction of chemicals and to reduce changing the structure of the mi­
crobial communities, pH adjustment was not performed during the 
whole AD process. After being loaded with inoculum, SM and NBW or 
DW, all reactors were sealed. N2 was then introduced for 3 min in all 
groups of reactors to ensure an initial anaerobic environment. After­
wards, all these groups of reactors were placed in an incubator at 35 ±
2 ◦C for about 42 days according to the preliminary experiments. All AD 
experiments were conducted in triplicate. 
2.1.3. Analytical methods 
In this work, the methane production from SM under different levels 
of ammonia inhibition was compared and analyzed. Total ammonia 
nitrogen (TAN), volatile solids (VS), and TS were measured by using the 
standard method (APHA, 2012). The methane content, pH value, the 
content of C, H, N, and S, soluble total organic carbon (STOC), volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs), free ammonia nitrogen (FAN), intermediate alka­
linity (IA), total alkalinity (TA), and partial alkalinity (PA) were 
analyzed according to a previous study (Fan et al., 2021). Soluble pro­
teins and soluble carbohydrates were analyzed by the Lowry method 
and the phenol–sulfuric method, respectively. The relative activities of 
three extracellular hydrolases, including acid phosphatase (ACP), alka­
line phosphatase (ALP), and α-glucosidase were determined on day 6 
based on a previous literature (Goel et al., 1998). In order to study the 
growth status of methanogens, coenzyme F420 was measured according 
to the previous reports at the end of the test (Dong et al., 2019; Dela­
fontaine et al., 1979). 
2.2. NBW preparation and characterization 
According to the previous work (Yang et al., 2019), Air-NBW was 
produced by applying a nano-bubble generation machine (HACK FB11, 
JAPAN). During the NBW production process, the preparation time was 
controlled at 20 min, and the pressure in NBW generator was kept at 
around 0.25 MPa. After that, NBW obtained from this nano-bubble 
generator was used throughout the whole AD process. NBW was char­
acterized based on the previously reported methods (Wang et al., 2019, 
Guo et al., 2019).

2.4. Statistical analysis 
Since NBW characteristics and the AD tests under different levels of 
ammonia inhibition were conducted in triplicate, mean value ± stan­
dard deviation (SD) were used for results and discussion. Statistical 
analysis was done using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) fol­
lowed by Tukey’s post-hoc test using Microsoft Excel 2019. The different 
letters (a, b, c, …) indicated the statistical significance (p < 0.05). Origin 
9.0 (Origin Lab) was also applied for the analysis and draw. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. TAN, FAN, and soluble organics 
Fig. 1a showed the changes of TAN with the supplementation of DW 
or NBW. AD process would be suppressed when TAN content exceeds 
3,000 mg/L (Bi et al., 2020). The difference in TAN content of RNBW and 
the corresponding control groups was not statistically significant (p >
0.05). Since R(0)NBW and R(0)Control did not exceed 1,000 mg/L, 
ammonia inhibition did not occur in these two groups. Severe ammonia 
inhibition also did not appear in R(1)Control and R(1)NBW because the 
TAN content of these two groups did not exceed 3,000 mg/L. R(3)NBW 
and the corresponding control group, however, showed ammonia inhi­
bition due to the TAN content higher than 3,500 mg/L. TAN content 
exceeding 6,000 mg/L appeared in R(5)Control and the corresponding 
control group, indicating that severe ammonia inhibition occurred in 
these two groups. The changes of FAN were shown in Fig. 1b. Obviously, 
FAN inhibition did not appear in R(0)Control and R(0)NBW because the 
FAN content of these two groups was <30 mg/L. According to a previous 
report, during AD process, the threshold for FAN inhibition was about 
80 mg/L (De Baere et al., 1984). As FAN content in R(3)NBW and the 
corresponding control group exceeded 90 mg/L and was significantly

higher than the other groups of reactors (p < 0.05) after 24 days, FAN 
inhibition occurred in these two groups. Although the TAN content of R 
(5)NBW and R(5)Control was higher than 6,000 mg/L, the FAN content of 
these two groups did not exceed 90 mg/L, which was caused by the 
lower pH value. As for R(1)NBW and R(1)Control, FAN inhibition might 
occur in the late AD process due to FAN content above 60 mg/L. 
The VFAs concentrations in all groups were shown in Fig. 2a and 
Fig. 2b. R(0)NBW and R(0)Control increased firstly and then decreased 
rapidly and VFAs accumulation did not occur during the whole AD 
processes. VFAs accumulation appeared in the early stage of AD in R 
(1)NBW and R(1)Control. On day 12, day 18, and day 24, R(1)NBW was 
lower than R(1)Control (p < 0.05). Combining with the results of methane 
production (Fig. 4), the lower VFAs concentrations in R(1)NBW may be 
due to higher consumption than that in R(1)Control. That was, NBW 
supplementation might promote the consumption of VFAs when 
ammonia suppression was not severe. The VFAs of R(3)NBW and the 
corresponding control group accumulated in the hydrolysis-acidification 
stage and then decreased in the methanation process. However, when 
the methanogenesis process was completely suppressed, the VFAs of R 
(5)Control and R(5)NBW could not be consumed during the AD processes. 
Therefore, NBW supplementation could not change the AD process 
failure when severe ammonia inhibition occurred. 
In the beginning, the concentrations of soluble proteins/carbohy­
drates in all groups were almost at the same level (Fig. 2c). The soluble 
proteins were first increased and then rapidly consumed in R(0)NBW and 
R(0)Control. Although the soluble proteins in R(3)Control and the corre­
sponding control group also decreased rapidly in the late stage of AD, 
these two groups were higher than that of R(0)NBW and R(0)Control. This 
phenomenon indicated that the higher TAN content was not conducive 
to the consumption of soluble protein. As for R(5)Control and R(5)NBW, the 
consumption of soluble protein was suppressed since the inhibition of 
AD process by high TAN content. The soluble proteins of R(0)NBW, R 
(1)NBW, and R(3)NBW were higher than the corresponding R(0)Control, R 
(1)Control, and R(3)Control on the 6th day. In terms of soluble carbohy­
drates, R(5)Control and R(5)NBW were also not consumed in large amounts 
during the AD process due to severe ammonia inhibition. Other groups, 
however, were gradually consumed as AD progressed, among which R 
(3)Control and R(3)NBW accumulated before being consumed. This was 
consistent with the performance of VFAs (Fig. 2a and Fig. 2b). 
Fig. 2d illustrated the changes in soluble TOC throughout the 42 
days’ AD process. Similarly, the soluble TOC contents of R(5)Control and 
R(5)NBW experienced an increasing firstly and was not consumed largely 
during the AD process. Other groups, however, firstly increased and then 
gradually consumed. It was worth noting that the final contents of R(3)

were higher than those of R(0) and R(1) (p < 0.05). A similar phe­
nomenon also appeared in the performance of VFAs (Fig. 2b). These 
phenomena occurred because ammonia inhibition was detrimental to 
the consumption of organics, resulting in a higher final soluble TOC and 
VFAs contents in R(3)NBW and the corresponding control group. In 
addition, the final VFAs contents of R(3)NBW were lower than that of the 
corresponding control group (p < 0.05), indicating that NBW supple­
mentation may promote the consumption of VFAs, which could also 
explain the significantly higher cumulative methane production in R 
(3)NBW compared to that of R(3)Control (Fig. 4). 
3.2. Buffering capacity of the AD process 
Since TA, IA, and PA are indicators for evaluating the stability during 
the AD process (Sun et al., 2016), these indicators were analyzed in this 
study. The changes in TA content under different levels of ammonia 
inhibition were shown in Fig. 3a. The TA of all groups increased to 
varying degrees, which was consistent with the change of pH value 
(Fig. 3e). The TA content of R(0)NBW and R(1)NBW were higher than the 
corresponding R(0)Control and R(1)Control, respectively on the 6th day (p 
< 0.05). In addition, on the 12th day, R(1)NBW and R(3)NBW were higher 
than the corresponding R(1)Control and R(3)Control, respectively (p <
0.05). These phenomena showed that during the early stages of AD 
process, NBW might benefit the increase in TA under ammonia inhibi­
tion. However, R(5)NBW and R(5)Control exhibited the lowest TA content, 
which was due to severe ammonia inhibition. Therefore, when severe 
ammonia inhibition occurred, NBW supplementation could not effec­
tively promote the buffering capacity of the AD system. 
PA content also experienced an upward trend in the early stage of AD 
(Fig. 3b). The relatively lowest PA content appeared in R(5)Control and R 
(5)NBW, which indicated that NBW supplementation could not promote 
the buffering capacity of AD system under severe ammonia inhibition. 
Comparison with R(0)Control and R(1)Control, on the 6th day, R(0)NBW and 
R(1)NBW showed a higher PA (p < 0.05), indicating that NBW was 
beneficial to the increase of PA and thus promoted the buffering ca­
pacity. Since IA/PA can be applied as a parameter to monitor the sta­
bility during the AD process (Yirong et al., 2017), this work also focused 
on the IA/PA ratio. All groups were reduced, except for R(5)NBW and R 
(5)Control (Fig. 3c). As for R(5)Control and R(5)NBW, the IA/PA ratio did not 
decrease significantly, which confirmed that the buffering capacity of 
these two groups was poor. 
Fig. 3d illustrated the changes in VFA/TA ratio. In the beginning, the 
VFA/TA ratio in RNBW and the corresponding RControl were almost at the 
same level. On the 6th day, the VFA/TA ratio in R(0)NBW gradually 
decreased, but other groups increased, indicating that R(0)NBW had the 
best-buffering capacity performance. The VFA/TA ratio of all groups 
gradually decreases with the AD process progressed except for R(5)NBW 
and R(5)Control . The VFA/TA of R(0)NBW and R(1)NBW were higher than 
the corresponding R(0)Control and R(1)Control, respectively on the 6th and 
12th day, and the difference was significant (p < 0.05). In addition, R 
(1)NBW and R(3)NBW were higher than the corresponding R(1)Control and 
R(3)Control, respectively on the 24th day, and the difference was also 
significant (p < 0.05). These similar phenomena further showed that 
NBW could promote the buffering capacity during the AD process. 
However, NBW supplementation could not promote the buffering ca­
pacity under sever ammonia inhibition. As an important parameter, pH 
is often applied for evaluating the buffering ability (Veluchamy et al., 
2019). All groups of reactors gradually increased, except for R(5)NBW 
and R(5)Control (Fig. 3e). This also showed that the AD processes of R 
(5)NBW and R(5)Control failed due to severe ammonia inhibition. 
The above results indicated that NBW supplementation could pro­
mote buffering capacity and alleviate slight ammonia inhibition. How­
ever, when TAN content was too high, the AD process was completely 
suppressed, and NBW supplementation could not change the failure of 
the AD process. This was because the supplementation of NBW to pro­
mote AD has a threshold in the case of ammonia inhibition. When the 
content of TAN and FAN was below the threshold, the supplementation 
of NBW could promote the AD process since the ammonia inhibition was 
not serious. However, when the content of TAN and FAN exceeded the 
threshold, the promotion effect of NBW was not enough to alleviate 
severe ammonia inhibition. Regarding the threshold at which NBW 
could significantly promote the AD process under ammonia inhibition, 
further research is needed. 
3.3. Methane production 
As shown in Fig. 4, when severe ammonia inhibition did not occur, 
the methane production from NBW groups were higher than that of 
control groups (p < 0.05). When TAN content exceeded 7,000 mg/L, the 
AD process of R(5)NBW and R(5)Control was inhibited. For the methane 
production, R(0)NBW, R(1)NBW and R(3)NBW obtained 218, 185 and 107 
mL/g-VS in the average, respectively, increasing by 15.3%, 12.3%,

38.7% in comparison to the corresponding control groups, respectively. 
In these eight groups, the maximum production of methane appeared in 
R(0)NBW. With the increasing of TAN, the yield of methane decreased. 
To better analyze the methane yield performance, the modified 
Gompertz model was used based on the previous research (Wang et al., 
2019). The results were showed in Table 2. The R(1)NBW and R(3)NBW 
showed a relatively shorter lag phase at a significant difference (p <
0.05) compared to those control groups. This result indicated that NBW 
significantly shorten the lag phase under ammonia inhibition. Obvi­
ously, the methane production performance of RNBW was better than the 
corresponding RControl, which could be confirmed by the higher Pmax 
value in RNBW. Moreover, in terms of Rmax, RControl was also significantly 
less than the RNBW (p < 0.05). These parameters were significantly 
promoted by NBW supplementation indicated that NBW supplementa­
tion enhanced the maximum methane production rate under ammonia 
suppression. 
3.4. Related enzyme 
During the AD process, hydrolysis is an essential stage because hy­
drolysis is considered the rate-limiting step (Yan et al., 2020). To reveal 
the application effect of NBW supplementation on the hydrolysis period 
under different levels of ammonia inhibition, this work evaluated three 
important extracellular hydrolases (ACP, ALP, and α-glucosidase). The 
relative activities of the three extracellular hydrolases in RNBW were 
higher than the corresponding RControl, indicating that NBW supple­
mentation could increase the activity of extracellular hydrolases to 
accelerate the hydrolysis process under ammonia inhibition (Fig. 5a). 
For the methanogenesis stage, the activity of methanogens has an 
important influence on this stage (Srisowmeya et al., 2020). Coenzyme 
F420 is a common coenzyme for methanogenic bacteria and can be used 
to determine the potential methanogenic bacterial activity in mixed 
microbial communities (Delafontaine et al., 1979). Clearly, the activity 
of coenzyme F420 with NBW supplementation was enhanced relative to 
the corresponding RControl (Fig. 5b). When the AD process progressed to 
the methanogenesis stage, the relatively high activity of coenzyme F420 
and the increased methane production in RNBW showed that the activity 
of methanogens was enhanced due to NBW supplementation under 
ammonia inhibition. Therefore, under ammonia inhibition, NBW could 
not only accelerate the hydrolysis process but also increase the activity 
of methanogens and further improve the methane production. 
3.5. Possible underlying mechanisms and application prospects 
This work confirmed that NBW supplementation could enhance 
methane production and relieve ammonia inhibition in ammonia-rich 
SM. NBW contains hundreds of millions of nano-bubbles (NBs) with a 
diameter of about a few hundred nm (Table 3), which are not available 
in DW. Moreover, the zeta potential of DW was lower than NBW for the 
absolute value, and the difference was significant (p < 0.05). The colloid 
has a stable system and avoids aggregation when zeta potential is high 
(Xiao et al., 2020). Therefore, NBW was more inclined to avoid the 
aggregation and maintain a stable system than DW, indicating that the 
stability of RNBW may be better relative to RControl. In addition, NBW has 
relatively longer spin–spin relaxation times (T2) and higher water 
molecule mobility compared to ordinary water (Liu et al., 2013; Fan 
et al., 2020a). Therefore, NBW with high water molecule mobility and 
high stability promoted the AD process under ammonia inhibition. In 
the hydrolysis stage, the enhanced hydrolase activity due to the sup­
plementation of NBW promoted the hydrolysis process. Moreover, NBW 
with higher mobility could improve nutrient mass transfer efficiency 
from liquid to bacterial cells (Wang et al., 2019). This was beneficial for 
improving the activity of microorganisms. Previous reports confirmed 
that the activity of Methanobacterium, Methanomassiliicoccus, Meth­
anospirillum, and Methanosaeta was enhanced due to the supplemen­
tation of NBW (Wang et al., 2020). This showed that the 
supplementation of NBW enhanced the activity of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens (HM) and acetoclastic methanogens (AM). 70% of

methane production comes from the AM pathway, and the remaining 
30% is contributed by the HM pathway (Yang et al., 2018). Although the 
proportion of methane production in the HM pathway is smaller than 
that of the AM pathway, the HM pathway can promote the mediation of 
biogasification under high ammonia conditions (Jiang et al., 2018). In 
addition, the HM pathway is the main pathway for methane production 
under ammonia inhibition (Yang et al., 2020b; Fotidis et al., 2013). 
Since the activity of HM was enhanced due to the supplementation of 
NBW, the mediating biogasification process may be promoted under 
ammonia inhibition. Therefore, despite the ammonia inhibition, the 
supplementation of NBW could promote methane production. The un­
derlying mechanisms of NBW promoting the AD process and relieving 
ammonia inhibition still need further research. 
This study indicated that NBW, as a novel method, can alleviate 
ammonia suppression and enhance methane yield. However, NBW could 
not change the poor methanogenesis performance when severe 
ammonia inhibition occurred (TAN > 7,000 mg/L). In addition, the 
increase in methane production under NBW supplementation was not 
high enough (from 12.3% to 38.7%) under ammonia inhibition. This 
was lower than the 54.6% achieved by using in-situ gas phase ammonia 
stripping (Yin et al., 2019), and was also lower than the 54.2% achieved 
by zero-valent iron addition (Yang et al., 2018). Although the increased 
amount in methane yield using the method of NBW supplementation 
was not high enough compared to other traditional methods, it enhances 
methane production with low-cost, environmentally friendly, and 
chemical-free. Moreover, the acquisition and application process of 
NBW does not require complicated equipment investment, huge energy 
consumption, or inconvenient operation techniques. With the contin­
uous development of NBW technology, it is foreseeable that the pro­
duction of NBW containing hundreds of millions or even billions of NBs 
concentrations will be realized. By then, NBW may not only greatly 
alleviate the ammonia inhibition, but also more effectively improve 
methane production compared to traditional methods. In addition, 
improving the application efficiency of NBW in the AD process, chang­
ing the application strategy of NBW, or combining NBW technology with 
optimized the parameters of AD process may also significantly increase 
the methane production under severe ammonia inhibition. Through the 
continuous innovation of NBW technology, the cost of applying NBW 
technology in the AD process to alleviate ammonia inhibition and in­
crease methane production will be greatly reduced. With the cost 
reduction, NBW technology will be widely used in the actual AD in­
dustry. Moreover, underdeveloped areas will be able to solve the prac­
tical problems of the AD process by applying low-cost NBW technology. 
Therefore, the application of NBW to solve the ammonia inhibition that 
often occurs in the AD process of SM has excellent potential and is 
worthy of further study. 
4. Conclusions 
This work demonstrated the effect of NBW supplementation in 
alleviating ammonia inhibition and enhancing methane production in 
ammonia-rich SM. Results indicated that NBW supplementation facili­
tated the rapid increase of TA and PA and the reduction of VFA/TA 
during the early stage of AD system, thus improved buffering capacity 
and alleviated ammonia inhibition. Besides, the cumulative methane 
production was enhanced by 12.3–38.7% via NBW supplementation 
even under ammonia inhibition. Moreover, the activities of hydrolase 
and coenzyme F420 were enhanced due to the supplementation of NBW, 
indicating the augmentation of hydrolysis and methanogenesis in the AD 
system.
